title: Real-World Asset Tokenization: $16T Opportunity
description: Learn how real-world asset tokenization works, why asset managers are testing it, and why experts see a trillion-dollar market.
alt: Blockchain tokens representing real world assets like bonds and funds

content.text: When BlackRock put a Treasury fund on Ethereum

BlackRock launched a tokenised money market fund called BUIDL in March 2024. The fund holds cash and short-term U.S. Treasury bills, and tokens on the Ethereum blockchain record who owns shares in it. Investors aren't buying a cryptocurrency in the usual sense. The token is a claim on a traditional financial instrument.

Within a few months the fund held hundreds of millions of dollars, and that scale got both traditional finance and the crypto industry talking. The launch also marked a change in what blockchains are being tested for. Early crypto projects created new digital assets. Tokenisation experiments use blockchain infrastructure to record ownership of assets that already exist.
What Tokenization of Real-World Assets Really Means

content.alt: Diagram showing how real world assets are tokenized on blockchain
content.caption: Tokenization links traditional assets, custodians, and blockchain-based ownership records.

content.text: Tokenising a real-world asset means turning ownership of something that exists outside the blockchain into tokens on it. Each token is a digital record showing a claim on part of the underlying asset. If a fund holds $100 million of government bonds, for example, it can issue tokens that each represent a small slice of that portfolio.

Transactions then move through blockchain transfers instead of traditional settlement systems. The underlying asset is still held by a custodian in the regular financial system. What changes is the record-keeping and the way ownership moves.
The idea is older than most cryptocurrency projects

People talked about digital securities long before decentralised finance became popular, and banks have explored electronic settlement for decades. What's changed in recent years is the infrastructure. Public blockchains let anyone verify records stored on the network, a feature that has caught the attention of crypto developers and banks alike. Several asset managers now run pilot programmes to see whether tokenised ownership can make settlement easier or distribution wider.
The idea is no longer just a theory

There are already products on the market. The BlackRock USD Institutional Digital Liquidity Fund holds short-term U.S. Treasuries, and tokens representing shares in the fund trade on Ethereum. Investors still have exposure to government debt, while the token records who owns what and lets holdings move across the network.

Franklin Templeton runs a U.S. government money fund, the Franklin OnChain U.S. Government Money Fund, that uses blockchain technology to track share ownership. The underlying assets are regular securities. Ondo Finance issues tokens backed by U.S. Treasury funds, which lets crypto investors hold exposure to government bonds directly. And MakerDAO, now known as Sky, has put part of its collateral into traditional assets such as short-term government securities through regulated intermediaries.
How big is it today?

Growth has been fast. Industry trackers such as rwa.xyz put the value of tokenised real-world assets at roughly $39 billion in September 2026, up sharply from only a few billion a couple of years earlier, with tokenised Treasuries and money market funds making up about $15.7 billion of it. BUIDL alone was around $2.7 billion at that point. Figures differ between trackers because they define "tokenised" differently, so treat any single number as approximate.
Why Banks and Governments Are Testing Tokenized Bonds

Tokenisation is also showing up in bond markets. The European Investment Bank issued a digital bond recorded on a blockchain network as part of a technology test, and other banks in Asia and Europe have run similar trials. The reason is practical, not ideological. Settling bonds the traditional way often involves many intermediaries, including brokers, clearing houses and custodians, while a blockchain system can record issuance and settlement on one shared ledger. Whether that reduces costs at scale is still being studied.
Estimates of the Size of the Market

Banks and consulting firms have tried to estimate how large tokenised assets could become. One much-quoted projection, from Boston Consulting Group and ADDX in 2022, put the figure at close to $16 trillion by 2030. Notice the gap between that and the roughly $39 billion on-chain today: the projection is a forecast of potential, not a measure of what exists, and forecasts like this have a long record of running ahead of reality. They're built from the size of existing financial markets.

content.alt: Visual showing the scale of tokenization opportunity across global asset markets
content.caption: Even a small shift of global real estate, bonds, and private markets onto blockchain could create a massive tokenized asset market.

content.text: These figures are rough and vary by source and year. If even a small part of these markets moved onto blockchain settlement, the tokenised total would be large. The estimate doesn't mean tokenisation will replace regular markets. It shows how big the addressable asset base already is.
What DeFi Protocols Want

At first, decentralised finance used cryptocurrencies as collateral. That created a circular system: people borrowed against crypto assets whose value swung widely. Real-world assets offer a different source of return. Government bonds, for example, pay interest that's easier to predict, and some DeFi platforms use them to back stablecoins or lending protocols. MakerDAO's exposure to Treasury bills is the best-known example, with part of its stablecoin backing coming from instruments that earn money outside crypto markets. Developers see this as a way to depend less on collateral that changes value.
What Tokenization Changes and What It Doesn't

Tokenisation doesn't change the economic nature of an asset. A token representing a Treasury bill still depends on the same government debt instrument. What differs is the record-keeping. In traditional markets, ownership records live in centralised databases run by banks and financial institutions. In a tokenised system a blockchain tracks who owns the tokens, and digital wallets, not brokers, handle transfers.
What infrastructure is needed for tokenized assets?

A tokenised asset system has several parts. A regulated custodian must hold the underlying asset. The tokens must legally correspond to the ownership claims they represent. And compliance procedures must decide who is allowed to hold or move them. In most current projects, blockchain tokens work alongside traditional financial systems rather than replacing them.
Limits That Are Still There

Tokenisation experiments remain small compared with the wider financial system. Legal systems need to be clear on how securities law treats tokenised ownership. Institutional investors usually want regulated custodians and vetted counterparties. And liquidity matters: a tokenised asset can only be traded if active buyers and sellers exist. Because of these obstacles, many projects are still pilots rather than full financial markets.
What Could Go Wrong for an Ordinary Investor

A token isn't automatically the same as legal ownership. Whether you have a claim on the underlying asset depends on how the product is structured, who the issuer is and where it's regulated, so read the documents, not the marketing. There's custodian and issuer risk, smart-contract risk, and the chance that you can't sell when you want to because few buyers exist. Many tokenised funds are also limited to qualified or institutional investors, so access may be restricted depending on where you live. And as with any crypto product, lookalike scams use the "real-world assets" label to sell worthless tokens. Treat anything promising fixed high returns from tokenised property or gold with suspicion.
Why People Are Talking About This Now

As decentralised finance grew, so did interest in tokenisation. Crypto developers started to ask whether blockchain systems could work with assets that aren't native to crypto, while banks and other financial institutions began exploring blockchain settlement as part of their technology research. The two trends met, and both groups are now trying the same idea: using distributed ledgers to track ownership. Regulation, infrastructure and market demand will all shape whether it goes mainstream.
Main Points

items: Tokenisation is a way to record ownership of traditional assets with blockchain tokens.
Asset managers and crypto protocols already run tokenised government bonds, funds and credit products, with tens of billions of dollars on-chain today.
Because global financial assets are so large, analysts see room for trillions of dollars of tokenised assets, but projections run well ahead of reality so far.
The technology doesn't change what the assets are. It changes how ownership and settlement are recorded.
Adoption is still gradual as banks test their systems and rules evolve.

faq.question: What is real-world asset tokenisation?
faq.answer: It's the process of representing ownership of an asset that exists outside the blockchain, such as a Treasury fund or a bond, as tokens on a blockchain. The underlying asset is still held by a custodian.

faq.question: Is the $16 trillion figure real?
faq.answer: It's a forecast for 2030 from Boston Consulting Group and ADDX, published in 2022, not a measure of today's market. Tracked tokenised assets are currently in the tens of billions of dollars.

faq.question: Can ordinary investors buy tokenised funds?
faq.answer: Sometimes. Many products are restricted to qualified or institutional investors, and access depends on the issuer, the platform and your country's rules.

faq.question: Does owning a token mean I own the underlying asset?
faq.answer: Not automatically. It depends on how the product is structured legally, who issues it and who holds the underlying asset, so read the offering documents.
